meta.location: Jershon, Antionum, Manti, and the river Sidon
principles: Armor as an advantage that shortens a war
The stated grounds for defensive war

world_behind.title: Mormon sets the preaching aside deliberately
world_behind.text: Verses 1 and 2 say Alma and his sons kept preaching and that he will say no more about it. Twenty-one chapters of war follow.

world_behind.title: This begins the longest continuous block in the record
world_behind.text: Alma 43 through 63 covers roughly eighteen years of fighting. The scale is why recurring war vocabulary has to be treated once and then deferred.

world_behind.title: Zerahemnah staffed his command with dissenters
world_behind.text: Verse 6 says the Amalekites were more murderous than the Lamanites, so he appointed Amalekites and Zoramites as chief captains to keep the hatred up.

world_behind.title: Mormon gives both sides' aims side by side
world_behind.text: Verses 7 and 8 give Zerahemnah's designs: usurp power, bring the Nephites into bondage. Verses 9 and 10 answer with land, family, freedom, and religion.

world_behind.title: The people of Ammon pay for the armies they will not join
world_behind.text: Verse 13 says they gave a large portion of their substance, and that the Nephites were compelled to fight alone. Alma 27 had set that arrangement up.

world_behind.title: Moroni is twenty-five
world_behind.text: Verse 17 gives his age at appointment. Mormon records it once and never returns to it.

world_behind.title: The armor decides the campaign before a battle
world_behind.text: Verses 19 through 22 have the Lamanites refuse to engage at Jershon because of breastplates and shields, and march around to Manti instead.

words.text: The Lamanite commander. The name occurs seventeen times, all in Alma 43 and 44, and never afterward. He is a Nephite dissenter leading an army against the country he left.

Shields worn on the arm. The compound occurs once in scripture. Mormon lists it between breastplates and head shields, and the whole equipment list is what stops the Lamanites from fighting at Jershon.
Treated at Mosiah 8:10, where Limhi's expedition brings back breastplates of brass and copper. Here they are Nephite issue, and the King James Bible uses the word only in Revelation, of locusts.

A plan made to deceive an enemy. The word occurs seven times in this record and never in the King James Bible, and six of the seven are in these war chapters. Mormon uses it here for the first time, of Moroni dividing his army to encircle the Lamanites.

Plate armor for the head. Six uses of the compound here, and none in the King James Bible. Verses 38 and 44 use it twice, once of what protected the Nephites and once of what the Lamanites smote in two.

Fierce creatures, in the King James Bible usually inhabitants of ruins. Treated at 2 Nephi 23:22. It appears three times in the record, and the King James Bible sixteen. Mormon uses it once as a simile for how the Lamanites fought under Zerahemnah's captains.

phrases.term: Alma, also, himself, could not rest
phrases.text: The last thing said of Alma before he leaves the record. Alma 45 gives his departure; here he is still going out to preach because he cannot sit still.
A whole people changes category in four words. Alma 35 ended with them stirring up the Lamanites; the war chapters open with the merger complete.

phrases.term: That they might worship God according to their desires
phrases.text: The last item in the Nephite list of aims, and the one Mormon expands in verse 10. He grounds the war in what the Lamanites would destroy rather than in what the Nephites would gain.

phrases.term: They had entered into a covenant and they would not break it
phrases.text: Mormon explains the people of Ammon in one clause. Their refusal is described as a promise held rather than as a policy, and it is why the Nephites fight alone.

phrases.term: He was only twenty and five years old when he was appointed chief captain
phrases.text: Moroni's age, given once. Mormon supplies it in the same verse that gives him all the command and the government of their wars.

phrases.term: They were naked, save it were a skin which was girded about their loins
phrases.text: The Lamanite army described by what it lacked. Mormon lists their weapons first and their clothing second, and verse 21 gives the effect: they were afraid despite outnumbering the Nephites.

phrases.term: Moroni, also, knowing of the prophecies of Alma, sent certain men unto him
phrases.text: A general consults a prophet about troop movements. Verse 24 has Alma report the Lamanite line of march, and the messengers carry it back.
Mormon's one simile for the Lamanite attack. It sits at the end of a verse listing what they broke: head-plates smitten in two, breastplates pierced, arms smitten off.

phrases.term: They were not fighting for monarchy nor power but they were fighting for their homes
phrases.text: Mormon states the Nephite cause by contrast with the enemy's. The list runs homes, liberties, wives, children, their all, rites of worship, and church.

phrases.term: Inasmuch as ye are not guilty of the first offense, neither the second, ye shall not suffer yourselves to be slain
phrases.text: The Lord quoted, giving the condition for defensive war. The permission depends on not having started it and not having escalated it.

phrases.term: Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed
phrases.text: The second half of the quotation, and the strongest thing in it. Mormon puts the whole justification of the Nephite war effort into two verses of quoted instruction.

verses.label: v. 2–3
verses.title: A subject dropped and another picked up, both announced
verses.text: The record marks its own transition in two consecutive sentences: "Now we shall say no more concerning their preaching," and then "And now I return to an account of the wars between the Nephites and the Lamanites." The first sentence still manages to summarize what it is declining to report, that they preached "according to the spirit of prophecy and revelation." From here to Alma 62 the record is almost entirely military, so this is the hinge of the book and it is stated as an editorial decision rather than concealed inside a narrative turn.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: An appointment policy explained by the motive behind it
verses.text: The record does not merely report who commanded. It gives the reasoning: the chief captains over the Lamanites "were all Amalekites and Zoramites," and the purpose was "that he might preserve their hatred towards the Nephites." Verse 8 then states the commander's own aims in two parts, to "usurp great power" over his own side and to gain power over the enemy. The record thus attributes the war to an internal political interest of the man who started it, and it does so before describing a single engagement.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: An age recorded for a commander
verses.text: The record supplies a number that nothing in the narrative requires: "he was only twenty and five years old when he was appointed chief captain over the armies of the Nephites." Ages are given rarely in these books, and mostly for kings at accession, as at Mosiah 6:4 and Mosiah 29:46. This one belongs to a military appointment, and the word "only" carries a judgment about it that the record does not otherwise explain.

verses.label: v. 23–24
verses.title: A prophet consulted as an intelligence source
verses.text: The record has the general do two things at once: send spies, and send messengers to Alma, "desiring him that he should inquire of the Lord whither the armies of the Nephites should go." The answer that comes back is tactical, naming a route and an objective, that the Lamanites "might come over into the land of Manti, that they might commence an attack upon the weaker part of the people." Revelation and reconnaissance are used side by side in the same sentence, with no comment on the pairing.

verses.label: v. 30
verses.title: A commander's ethical reasoning entered into the record
verses.text: The record reports not just the stratagem but the judgment behind it: "he thought it no sin that he should defend them by stratagem." The verb is deliberate, and the clause is attached to the reasons given in verses 29 and 30, the enemy's intent to establish a kingdom against the Nephites' desire to keep lands, liberty, and church. Nothing in the narrative asks the question the sentence answers. It is the record supplying a defense of deception in war before anyone objects.

verses.label: v. 45–47
verses.title: A rule of engagement quoted as scripture
verses.text: The record gives the Nephite cause in the negative first, "they were not fighting for monarchy nor power," and then supplies two quoted rules. The first sets a threshold: "Inasmuch as ye are not guilty of the first offense, neither the second, ye shall not suffer yourselves to be slain by the hands of your enemies." The second states a duty: "Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed." Neither appears earlier in the record as spoken to anyone; both are introduced here as things "the Lord had said unto them, and also unto their fathers." A war narrative pauses to cite a law that the surviving text does not otherwise contain.

chapter.title: Mormon states both war aims before any fighting
chapter.text: Seven verses of motive precede the first engagement. The reader is given what each side wanted before being shown what each side did.

chapter.title: The pacifists finance the army
chapter.text: The people of Ammon will not fight and give a large portion of their substance instead. Mormon records the arrangement plainly and calls the Nephites compelled to fight alone.

chapter.title: Armor changes the campaign without a battle
chapter.text: The Lamanites see the equipment and march twenty miles around. The first tactical event of the war block is a refusal to engage.

chapter.title: A general asks a prophet where the enemy is going
chapter.text: Moroni sends spies and a messenger to Alma in the same verse. Mormon shows revelation and reconnaissance used together and ranks neither.

chapter.title: Mormon quotes the Lord to justify the war
chapter.text: Verses 46 and 47 supply two quoted rules and attribute both to speech rather than to reasoning. One of them fixes a condition, "Inasmuch as ye are not guilty of the first offense, neither the second, ye shall not suffer yourselves to be slain by the hands of your enemies." The second states a duty, "Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed." Neither sentence is attributed to any earlier speaker in the surviving text, and Mormon 4:4 later uses the first of them to explain a defeat.

chapter.title: The turning point is a thought, not a maneuver
chapter.text: Verse 48 has the men about to flee and Moroni inspiring their hearts with their lands and freedom. Verse 50 says the Lamanites broke in that selfsame hour.

chapter.title: The victory ends in an order to stop
chapter.text: The last verse gives the order and its trigger together: "Moroni, when he saw their terror, commanded his men that they should stop shedding their blood." Verse 51 has just recorded the enemy as "more numerous, yea, by more than double the number of the Nephites" and surrounded on both sides of the river. The chapter that opens twenty chapters of war ends with the winning commander stopping while the enemy is encircled, and Alma 44 spends its first eleven verses on the terms he offers instead.

chapter.title: The war vocabulary is laid down here
chapter.text: Stratagem, arm-shields, head-plates, and breastplates all arrive in one chapter. Alma 43 is where these terms get their treatment for the twenty chapters that follow.

applications.title: Say what you are for before you say what you oppose
applications.text: Mormon states the Nephite aim first, "to support their lands, and their houses, and their wives, and their children," and only then the enemy's design. A cause described in terms of what it protects is a different thing from one described in terms of what it hates.

applications.title: Pay for what you will not do yourself
applications.text: The people of Ammon would not fight and "did give unto the Nephites a large portion of their substance to support their armies." A conviction that costs you nothing is worth examining; theirs was expensive and they paid it in a form they could give.

applications.title: Prepare people as well as ground
applications.text: The armour is described in detail and so is the morale work, "Moroni, perceiving their intent, sent forth and inspired their hearts with these thoughts—yea, the thoughts of their lands, their liberty." Equipment and reasons are both listed as preparation.

applications.title: Ask and scout
applications.text: Moroni sent spies into the wilderness and sent to Alma to inquire of the Lord, in the same verse. Two kinds of information gathered at once, and the record treats neither as a substitute for the other.

applications.title: Cover the place you are leaving
applications.text: He leaves part of the army in Jershon "lest by any means a part of the Lamanites should come into that land." Moving to meet the threat you have identified should not open the position you already hold.

applications.title: Decide in advance what would justify it
applications.text: Two quoted rules set the threshold before the fighting: not guilty of the first offense nor the second, and "Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed." Write down the conditions while you are calm.

applications.title: Remind people what they are defending
applications.text: At the point of breaking, what turns the line is a reminder rather than an order, and verse 49 has them cry "unto the Lord their God, for their liberty and their freedom from bondage." Naming the stake is a practical intervention.

applications.title: Stop when the point is made
applications.text: "Moroni, when he saw their terror, commanded his men that they should stop shedding their blood." The enemy is surrounded and outnumbered and the order is to stop. Decide in advance what winning is, so you can recognise it when it arrives.

questions.text: What can I not rest from, and is it the right thing?
Who benefits from keeping me angry?
What covenant of mine would cost me if I kept it?
What am I giving to a cause I cannot join?
What was I trusted with young, and how did I handle it?
Am I fighting for something, or against someone?
When have I had the advantage and chosen to stop?
